Kinetic study on the effects of elevated temperature and micro aeration in 
volatile fatty acids production by anaerobic fermentation of 
alkaline-pretreated oil palm empty fruit bunch

A B S T R A C T   
This research studied the conversion of alkaline-pretreated oil palm empty fruit bunch (OPEFB) into volatile fatty 
acids (VFA) through anaerobic fermentation (AF). In AF, the methanogens that consume VFAs must be sup­
pressed to increase the accumulated VFA as an intermediate product of AF. In-depth research has not been 
conducted on the effects of temperature and micro aeration to maximize the VFA accumulation. To investigate 
the temperature effect, the experiment was run at mesophilic (RM) and thermophilic conditions (RT). The impact 
of the micro aeration dose was studied in the thermophilic reactor set to the ORP −50 mV (RTM −50) and ORP 
−150 mV (RTM −150). The experimental data were fitted to the Anaerobic Digestion Model 1 (ADM 1) using 
AQUASIM®. The khyd.ch value of the RT reactor is higher than that of the RM, suggesting that high temperatures 
encourage hydrolysis and enhance hydrolase activity. Based on the simulation results, RT reactors without micro- 
aeration had a substantially higher specific growth rate of methanogens compared to RM. Therefore, micro 
aeration should be applied in RT to suppress the potentially faster growth of methanogen bacteria at elevated 
temperature. The result of this study indicated that both temperature and micro-aeration were important process 
variable to be further optimized to make VFAs production from OPEFB attractive.   
1. Introduction 
Over the last few decades, palm oil production has grown very 
rapidly. Consequently, the amount of oil palm empty fruit bunch 
(OPEFB) as the solid wastes in palm oil industries has increased signif­
icantly, posing a severe environmental burden. Based on Indonesia’s 
Central Statistical Bureau (Badan Pusat Statistik/BPS) data, in 2020, 
Indonesia produced more than 44 million tons of palm oil annually [1]. 
For every ton of fresh fruit bunches used in the oil extraction process, 
lignocellulosic biomass was produced, including oil palm empty fruit 
bunches (OPEFB) (23%), mesocarp fiber (12%), decanter cake (6%), and 
shell (5%) [2]. Untreated OPEFB contained 15.2% hemicellulose, 25.8% 
lignin, 40.9% cellulose, and 18.1% miscellaneous components [3]. The 
rich carbon source in lignocellulosic biomass makes it a highly ideal 
substrate feedstock for anaerobic processes, which produce carboxylic 
acids and biogas [4,5]. However, before being used as a substrate, 
OPEFB must be pretreated because lignin in the biomass forms an 
impermeable/resistant layer, making it difficult to biodegrade [6]. In 
another study, pretreated OPEFB could be a source of fermentable 
sugars [7], such as 2,3-butanediol (2,3-BDO). Other interesting pathway 
of utilizing lignocellulose waste is anaerobic fermentation (AF) to collect 
the intermediate product, i.e. volatile fatty acids (VFA) [8,9]. 
VFAs are low-molecular-weight carboxylates containing 2–6 carbon 
atoms with primary components of propionic acid, acetic acid, butyric 
acid, and valeric acid [10]. Some of the potential substrates to produce 
VFAs include citrus waste [11], activated sludge waste [12], tuna waste 
[13], household food waste [14], and vegetable waste [15]. VFAs can be 
utilized as attractive carbon sources for the removal of ammonia, ni­
trogen, and phosphorus during wastewater treatment [16,17]. They can

also be transformed into various biochemicals required in various in­
dustries [18]. VFAs are particularly valuable in the chemical industry as 
precursors for synthesizing esters, aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, and 
alkanes [14]. VFAs can also be used to grow a lipid-accumulating 
oleaginous yeast (i.e., Apiotrichum porosum DSM27194) which can 
further be used as a fuel feedstock for oleochemicals production [19]. 
Anaerobic fermentation has recently become a cost-effective and 
environmentally acceptable method of producing VFAs [20–22]. From a 
metabolic perspective, the AF pathways consist of two main routes, i.e. 
acidogenic fermentation and methanogenesis [23]. Complex organic 
polymers are broken down into simple soluble monomers in the first 
phase of the AF process, called hydrolysis, by extracellular enzymes 
produced by hydrolytic microbes [24]. Acidogenic bacteria convert the 
products generated during hydrolysis to volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and 
minor products such as hydrogen and carbon dioxide (CO2). Methano­
genic bacteria consume the products of acidogenesis and acetogenesis 
and produce carbon dioxide and methane in the final phase [25]. 
Therefore, when the AF purpose is to produce VFAs, the challenge is 
maximizing the accumulation of the VFAs by preventing the consump­
tion of the VFAs by the methanogenes. Meanwhile, increasing the 
acidification rate is also still challenging [26]. In addition, when dealing 
with the raw material which is difficult to disintegrade, some special 
treatments might be necessary, such as the addition of strong oxidizer 
[17]. 
Several studies reported the effect of temperature on VFA production 
from anaerobic fermentation. Garcia-Aguirre et al. [27] concluded that 
VFA production from organic waste was slightly higher in the process 
with an acidic pH at thermophilic condition (55 ◦C). Increasing the 
temperature and pH accelerated hydrolysis due to increased particulate 
solubilization [28,29]. To maximize VFA accumulation, the metha­
nogens that consume VFAs should be inhibited [30]. Methanogens are 
sensitive to environmental variation and various factors, including 
temperature and micro oxygenation, that could inhibit the activity of 
methanogens. Recent investigations have shown the benefit of using 
micro aeration in hydrolytic-acidogenic reactors to dissolve organic 
substrates, including food waste [31], mixed sludge [32], and Napier 
grass [33]. Micro aeration is the controlled addition of minute amounts 
of oxygen to an anaerobic biochemical process. It allows anaerobic and 
aerobic biological activity in a single bioreactor [34]. Sawatdeenarunat 
et al. [9] reported the maximum VFAs yield of 107.3 2.6 mg/gVSadded 
was obtained at 15 mL O2 addition per gVSadded, three days of incuba­
tion, with anaerobically digested cattle manure (ADCM) as an inoculum. 
Micro oxygenation may be an environmentally beneficial method to 
increase the yields of VFAs from lignocellulosic feedstocks for producing 
high-value chemicals and bioenergy [9]. According to Lim et al. [29], 
the advantage of micro aeration was to change the fermentation pro­
duction pattern where acetic acid was converted into butyric acid. 
Compared to the non-aerated settings, the AF system with micro aera­
tion has more varied bacterial communities. The authors also noted that 
a micro aerated AF system had a higher percentage of populations from 
the Firmicutes phylum than an anaerobic system, which led to a faster 
rate of substrate hydrolysis. 
Precise oxygen dose control is required to avoid oxygen overdosage. 
Oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) can be a precise parameter for 
controlling the proper micro aeration dosage since it measures the net 
value of all complex oxidation-reduction reactions in an aqueous envi­
ronment [35]. The redox potential is measured by the ORP, which is also 
sensitive to oxygen in an aqueous solution [36]. Thus, ORP can be used 
to define the condition of biochemical reactions [35]. According to 
Nguyen et al. [37], as soon as the ORP-controlled micro aeration (at ORP 
of −470 mV) was started, the total VFA concentration quickly dropped 
to 3.0 g HAc/L, the methane output increased, and oxygen served as the 
limiting electron acceptor for the facultative heterotrophs. According to 
Yin et al. [26], the ideal ORP level for VFA synthesis was between −100 
and −200 mV. Low oxygen resulted in a high yield and higher pro­
portions of facultative acidogenic bacteria (phylum Firmicutes, Proteo­
bacteria, etc.). 
The entire AF process is better understood with the help of mathe­
matical models, which can also be used to simulate the changes at each 
process stage [38]. This study evaluated the data using Anaerobic 
Digestion Model No.1 (ADM1) created by an International Water Asso­
ciation (IWA) work group. The model could increase the understanding 
of the process configuration, such as the primary biochemical reactions 
and physico-chemical processes in AF fermentation [39]. The ADM1 is a 
structural model that includes the processes of disintegration, hydroly­
sis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis. A total of 19 pro­
cesses, 24 components, and 56 stoichiometric and kinetic parameters are 
developed for the biological processes involved. As an all-purpose pro­
cess model, ADM1 can enhance lab-scale and full-scale plant design 
applications and directly apply them to large-scale plants. 
A modified ADM1 has been developed by Bai et al. [40] to simulate 
substrate degradation and the impact of pH on the production of VFAs. 
Three substrate degradation models were compared for protein and 
carbohydrate degradations, including first-order kinetics, i.e., Monod 
and Contois. The Monod model most accurately approximated the sol­
uble protein and carbohydrate breakdown. The simulated ADM1 by 
AQUASIM® well predicted the VFA production and the inhibition effects 
during simulation. A previous study tested oxygen effects in AF

This study was aimed to investigate VFA production from OPEFB by 
increasing temperature and inhibiting methane formation. OPEFB is a 
complex substrate which needs a combination of elevated temperature 
and an optimum dose of micro aeration in the AF to maximize the VFA 
accumulation. The effect of thermophilic temperature and ORP- 
controlled micro aeration has never been tested on the VFA accumula­
tion optimization and on the microbial population dynamics in the AF of 
OPEFB substrate. This study was conducted on the AF of alkaline-treated 
OPEFB. The AF was firstly operated at mesophilic and thermophilic 
conditions to confirm the effectiveness of the elevated temperature. 
Secondly, the AF was conducted at the thermophilic conditions with 
varied micro aeration intensities. The micro aeration level was varied 
based on the measured ORP. The treatment comparison in the current 
study was based on ADM1’s kinetic constant values. The AQUASIM® 
software was used to determine the ADM1 kinetics parameters. All 
parameter values were initially taken from ADM1 defaults for parame­
ters to be estimated. The adjustable parameters are related to the 
microorganism properties, i.e., khyd.ch, km.bu, km.pro, km.ac, Ks.bu, Ks.pro, 
and Ks.ac. The differences between the data-fitted constant and the 
default values will reveal the unique features of the investigated process, 
which may be necessary for scale-up consideration. The high- 
throughput 16 s rRNA sequencing was used for microbial identifica­
tion to cross-check the indications inferred by the model constants from 
the data fitting on ADM1. The result of this study is useful to recommend 
the appropriate temperature and ORP values which maximize the VFA 
accumulation. 
2. Material and method 
2.1. Inoculum and substrate 
Digested cow manure (DCM) was used as the inoculum. The inoc­
ulum was taken from the effluent of a mesophilic biogas reactor running 
on cow manure feedstock in Kaliurang, Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The total 
plate count (TPC) analysis of the anaerobic bacteria in DCM revealed 
that the viable cell concentration was 16,000 mg cell.L−1. The oil palm 
empty fruit bunches (OPEFB) were obtained from the palm oil industry 
in Medan, North Sumatra Province, Indonesia. Sun-dried OPEFB was 
chopped and ground into less than 0.42 mm average diameter particles. 
Untreated OPEFB containing 40.09 ± 0.01%-w glucan, 23.94 ± 0.01%- 
w hemicellulose, 21.77 ± 0.01%-w lignin, and 3.72 ± 0.07%-w ash. 
Furthermore, the NREL/TP510–42,620 [42] technique was used to 
determine the total solid (TS) and volatile solids (VS) of the OPEFB. In 
addition, the OPEFB was delignified using a chemical method (NaOH, 
8% w/v) at 100 ℃ for one hour [43]. Table 1 presents the substrate and 
inoculum specifications used in this study. 
2.2. Batch reactor assembly 
The pretreated OPEFB and the inoculum with a ratio of 1:1 (VS/VS) 
were mixed in a beaker glass and put into a 1000 mL batch reactor 
(Wheaton Spinner Flask, DWK Life Sciences, USA). The amount of the 
substrate and inoculum mixture was 75% of the reactor volume. The 
initial pH was set to 5.5 using 1 M NaOH or 1 M HCl. Nitrogen was 
bubbled into the liquid before the reactor hose was connected to the 
gasometer. Each test condition was run in duplicates, and the measured 
parameters were averaged for the final evaluation. 
The first set of the experiments were run in mesophilic and ther­
mophilic conditions. The second set of the experiments were carried out 
in thermophilic condition with and without micro aeration. The micro 
aeration was controlled at the ORP values of −50 mV and −150 mV. The 
micro aeration scheme is shown in Fig. 1. The airflow rate from the auto 
aerator (Jebao, DP-4, China) was set using a digital timer and auto­
matically connected to the probed ORP controller (Mettler Toledo, Co­
lumbus, Ohio, USA). The micro aeration intensity (LO2/L reactor/day) 
was calculated by multiplying the oxygen flow rate by the daily micro 
aeration time and dividing it by the working volume of the reactor. A 
gasometer was connected to the reactor to detect biogas formation. 
Nevertheless, we did not observe any biogas formation during the study. 
Therefore, no biogas data was presented. 
2.3. Analytical method 
Four operating conditions were evaluated in this study (Table 2). 
Two reactors, i.e., Mesophilic Reactor (RM) and Thermophilic Reactor 
(RT), were used to study the effect of temperature. Meanwhile, to assess 
the impact of micro aeration dose, three reactors were used at thermo­
philic condition, namely the thermophilic reactor without aeration (RT), 
the thermophilic reactor with aeration at the ORP value of −50 mV 
(RTM −50), and the thermophilic reactor with aeration at the ORP value 
of −150 mV (RTM −150). All experimental setups were carried out in 
duplicates for 16 days. The experiment was stopped when the total sCOD 
and VFA concentrations did not significantly change anymore. 
The parameters observed during the experiment were total chemical 
oxygen demand (CODt) and soluble chemical oxygen demand (CODs), 
pH, and VFA concentration. The pH and ORP values are monitored using 
an electrode (Mettler Toledo, Columbus, Ohio, USA) connected to the 
reactor system. Samples were centrifuged at 11,000xg for 5 min to 
separate the fermented broth from the residue. Total solids (TS) and 
volatile solids (VS) of inoculum and reactor effluent were determined 
based on the standard analytical procedures by APHA-AWWA-WEF 
[44]. The CODs and CODt were determined according to the closed 
reflux method 5220 D [44]. The Hach kit (DR 900, Loveland, Colorado, 
USA) was used to conduct the CODt and CODs colourimetric analysis. 
The initial microbial amount of the inoculum was determined using 
anaerobic total plate count [45]. The 16 s rRNA assay was used to 
determine the ratio of each variable (Xsu, Xbu, Xpro, Xac) in order to 
determine the composition of the microbial community. 
The VFAs were determined using a gas chromatograph (Perkin- 
Elmer, Shelton, CT, USA) with a capillary column (Elite-WAX ETR, 
Perkin-Elmer, Shelton, CT, USA) and a flame-ionized detector (Perki­
nElmer, Shelton, CT, USA). Injection and detection temperatures were 
250 and 300 degrees Celsius, respectively. Nitrogen served as the carrier 
gas at two mL.min−1 flow rate and a pressure of 20 psi. Each injection 
capacity was 1 µL. Each standard volatile free acid mix (Sigma-Aldrich) 
was dissolved in water to make a stock solution of caproic acid, iso- 
valeric acid, valeric acid, iso-butyric acid, butyric acid, propionic acid, 
and acetic acid. A 10 g.L−1 mixed stock standard solution was prepared 
by combining the two solutions.

2.4. Microbial diversity analyses 
Digested samples of both liquid and solid phases were collected using 
a conical tube and immediately frozen at −20 ℃. The sample was 
placed at room temperature to melt before running the total DNA 
analysis. As much as 250 µL of liquid phase sample and 0.5 mg solid- 
phase was utilized to extract the total microbial DNA with Zymo 
Research Quick-DNA™ Fecal/Soil Microbe Miniprep Kit D6010 (Zymo 
Research, United States). DNA isolation was carried out in three stages: 
lysis, precipitation, and purification/elution. NanoDrop2000 with the 
dsDNA program was used to determine the concentration and the purity 
of DNA, while agarose gel electrophoresis was conducted to detect the 
DNA integrity and fragment size. The 16 S rRNA gene segments were 
amplified through PCR reactions using the primer 341-F (5′-CCT AYG 
GGR BGC ASC AG-3′) and 806-R (5′-GGA CTA CNN GGG TAT CTA AT- 
3′) to both bacteria and archaea and then, sequenced on Illumina 
NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina, United States) by NovogeneAIT Ge­
nomics Singapore Pte. (Singapore). 
The diversity and species richness indices were calculated using the 
rRNA Database Project (SILVA database at http://www.arb-silva.de/). 
Based on the richness estimate of the Simpson [46] and Shannon [47] 
indices, an OTU-based alpha diversity study was performed to investi­
gate bacterial diversity. The number of sequences divided by the total 
number of rows per sample was used to determine the relative abun­
dance for dominance hierarchy variables (%). 
2.5. Kinetic model for batch reactor 
The Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) is a model that 
comprehensively includes all compounds in anaerobic reaction mecha­
nisms validated by International Water Association (IWA) based on 
various scientific publications and industrial data. Not all aspects of the 
model always occur in every anaerobic process, so it is necessary to 
make appropriate assumptions for a particular case. The model’s accu­
racy depends on the accuracy of the assumptions taken in representing 
specific cases. 
The ADM1 distinguishes between biochemical and physicochemical 
mechanisms in anaerobic fermentation reactions. The first is biologi­
cally mediated, describing the four phases of anaerobic fermentation as 
they relate to the growth and decay of the bacteria engaged in the 
process. Instead, liquid-liquid, liquid–gas, and acid-base reactions are 
depicted in the physicochemical model. For each biochemical/chemical 
compound used in the simulation, the ADM1 allows the user to design a 
first-order differential equation. This equation depicts the change in 
concentration of the specific component under consideration over time 
while accounting for other compounds’ concentrations. The differential 
equation is developed using the Petersen matrices [48], which provide

and c (specified with v) of each subprocess. for this experiment (batch

3. Result and discussion 
3.1. VFA production 
The profiles of the CODs concentration and the total VFA yield, 
which reflect OPEFB hydrolysis and acidification at mesophilic and 
thermophilic conditions, are shown in Fig. 3(a) (RM) and 3(b) (RT). The 
CODs concentrations in each reactor (RM and RT) showed an upward 
trend at the beginning of the experiment and then stabilized with the 
extended fermentation time. The organic content removal is expressed 
as the total solid (TS) reduction displayed in Table 3. Total solid removal 
of thermophilic reactors is higher than mesophilic reactors. This data 
shows that thermophilic condition promotes hydrolysis and improves 
hydrolase activity [50] to make the acidogenic bacteria more efficiently 
convert the organic compounds into VFAs. In this study, the total VFA 
(TVFA) yield was enhanced at a temperature of 55 ℃, and a similar 
condition was reported by Huang et al. [51], who observed the highest 
VFA yield at 55 ℃. On the contrary, in the reactors with microaeration, 
lower TS removal was observed. However, in RTM-150, although the TS 
removal was lower than RM and RT, the VFA production was similar to

Bacteriodota is commonly found in completely anaerobic conditions,

close to the experimental data. Hence, the values of the adjustable ki­
netic constants could be used as the comparison tool to evaluate the

parameters in the kinetics of the AF process that shows how fast the 
maximum growth of microorganisms at each stage is. The µmax value of 
methanogen microorganisms is obtained by multiplication of km,ac and

communities of methanogenic microorganisms in RT reactors were 
higher when compared to RM reactors. With micro aeration, the μmax

presence of oxygen with ORP values of −50 to −150 mV inhibited 
methanogenic growth. This statement is also supported by the microbial

maximize the process of forming VFAs at the stage of acidogenesis. 
4. Conclusion 
In summary, this work study the effect of elevated temperature and 
micro-aeration on the amount of accumulated VFAs in the AF of 
alkaline-pretreated OPEFBs. It was found that: 1) the thermophilic 
condition benefited hydrolysis and enhanced hydrolase activity as 
shown by the higher khyd.ch value in RT than in RM. On the other hand, 
the hydrolysis and acidification processes did not benefit from micro 
aeration, 2) The hydrolytic microbial population was substantially more 
dominant in the RTM-50 and RTM-150 reactors compared to RT, the 
hydrolysis rates did not look appreciably different from those in RT 
reactors, 3) Mesophilic condition favored more buildup of propionate. In 
contrast, higher temperatures led to the accumulation of longer fatty 
acids, besides the higher production of acetic acid. The buildup of 
butyrate was more significant in the RT reactor than in the RM reactor. 
More diverse VFA individuals were discovered in reactors with micro 
aeration in the RT. N-butyric, iso-butyric, valeric, and iso-valeric acids 
were only found in RTM −50 and RTM −150, 4) The selection of 
facultative microorganisms was favored by micro aeration, and an 
adaptive functional flora was gradually enriched as a result. The absence 
of methanogenic bacteria in the reactors with micro aeration demon­
strated that keeping the ORP value between −50 and −150 mV inhibi­
ted the methanogens, 5) Based on the simulation results, RT reactors 
without micro-aeration induced higher specific growth rate of metha­
nogens compared to RM. Therefore, while the experimenal data showed 
that micro-aeration did not positively affect the hydrolysis and acido­
genesis rate, micro aeration at an optimized dosage should be applied in 
RT to suppress the potentially rapid growth of methanogen bacteria at 
elevated temperature.
